text: This lesson closes Chapter 2 by covering the final three guiding principles together, since they work as a tightly connected set rather than three separate ideas.

First, Think and Work Holistically. No service, practice, or team operates in isolation — a change to one part ripples outward whether anyone planned for it or not. A new field added to an incident form affects reporting, affects the knowledge base template, and affects any automation already reading that form's data. None of these effects are exotic; they're just easy to miss if a team only looks at its own corner of the system.

Second, Keep It Simple and Practical. If a process step, a metric, or a report doesn't add value, eliminate or simplify it rather than defending it just because it already exists. ITIL 4 favors the minimum number of steps needed to accomplish an objective. A five-approval sign-off chain for a low-risk change usually isn't more careful than a one-approval chain — it's just slower, with the extra approvers rubber-stamping something they don't have the context to meaningfully evaluate.

Third, Optimize and Automate, in that specific order. Automating a process that's fundamentally broken just makes the broken process execute faster and fail more consistently. A manual approval step that exists only because of a tool limitation that's since been fixed shouldn't be automated into permanence — it should be removed. Automation earns real value on work that's high-volume, repeatable, and well-defined, but only once it's already been assessed and streamlined.

These three principles close out the set because each one leans on something established earlier. Holistic thinking needs the investigation from Start Where You Are. Simplifying confidently needs the visibility that Collaborate and Promote Visibility provides. And safe automation needs the feedback loops that Progress Iteratively With Feedback establishes to catch a bad assumption before it's locked into code.

Seven guiding principles, designed to be applied together on any real decision, not picked one at a time. Next up: Chapter 3 begins, starting with the Plan, Improve, and Engage activities of the Service Value Chain.
